name: Carlos Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal day at your accounting firm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Carlos, 27, and I lead a three-person accounts team even though I still feel new some mornings. I have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I check tax returns, untangle client records, then call owners about the numbers. I like finding the one entry that explains a whole mess, but late corrections can eat the evening.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do work and money sit with you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI checks every day and enjoy testing new tools, though I never let them sign a return for me. I am paid below the usual rate for this work, have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar jobs nearby. My flatmate Lea and I split rent, and I keep meaning to ask my manager Mira for a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is nearly how my morning checks work now. I can picture a tax season where the client calls are still mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the firm I would say the software saves us a little typing, and our clients still need a person to sign off their accounts. The tax return still lands on my desk on Friday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I cannot afford a quiet month even without a technology shock. I lead three people at 27, but the firm pays me below the usual rate and I have less than a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the team on its current accounts and use the AI checks I already run each morning. Starting this November I would move a fixed slice of each pay cheque into a separate rent buffer, even if it is only a small slice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel busy rather than frightened by the software. The rent standing order still gives me a jolt every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that little saving look like by next spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no raise, perhaps I can build two weeks of rent by spring. I will not pretend a budgeting app makes up for low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to about pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my manager Mira the client corrections I caught this quarter and ask for a salary review in January. There are few accounting firms nearby, so I want the conversation before I threaten to leave.

say: I would tell colleagues **client sign-off** still needs an accountant even if routine entry gets faster.
I would tell colleagues the **Friday returns** still land on my desk despite a little faster routine entry.
think: I am a young **team lead** on low pay, and one bad month would empty my account.
I think the software is useful, but my **rent** is the immediate problem.
do: Keep our **current accounts** moving while I check AI flags each morning.
Move a small **pay slice** into a rent buffer each payday.
Ask Mira for a **salary review** in January using client corrections.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about rent despite steady work.
S0.quote: The rent standing order still gives me a jolt every month.
fieldNote: He treats the small software gain as ordinary, while **low pay** and almost no savings drive his private worry.
His plan to ask for a raise is grounded in **client corrections**, not an assumption that another local firm will hire him.

steps.text: Keep the team on its current client accounts
Move a pay slice into a separate rent buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the first real pressure on our review team. I would want to see the staffing plan beside the new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the staff that checking, drafting returns, and answering client questions are changing first, so we should check the system instead of hiding it. I already use AI every day, but I would not call a smaller trainee intake good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the firm keeping me to review exceptions while dropping a junior vacancy. My own post could narrow to one reviewer for several teams, and I cannot carry a mortgage-sized gap with less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I would ask Mira for a paid audit-trail course and take it if she approves, then spend Friday afternoons testing the tools on old returns with client details removed. If the firm refuses paid time, I would complete one free course at home rather than buy an expensive certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert, and also guilty about the trainees. Being the quickest with a tool does not make the lost vacancy harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which vacancy are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm planned to replace a trainee who left in September, and Mira has said the requisition is on hold. I would ask whether the saved budget can fund the training time instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would update my CV, but the nearby firms are few and may be freezing the same posts. I would apply only if an actual reviewer vacancy appears with a higher stated salary.

say: I would tell my team **checking work** changes first, so we must learn where the software gets returns wrong.
I would ask management to put the held **trainee budget** into paid review training.
think: I suspect one reviewer could cover **several teams**, including mine.
I cannot absorb a sudden **pay gap** with less than a month saved.
do: Take **paid audit training** if Mira approves, or complete a free course at home.
Test AI tools on **old returns** with client details removed each Friday.
Apply only for a **higher-paid** reviewer vacancy if one appears nearby.
feel: I feel **anxious** for my own post and the held trainee place.
S1.quote: Being the quickest with a tool does not make the lost vacancy harmless.
fieldNote: His public case for training also exposes a **specific held vacancy** at the firm.
He is willing to search, but **few local firms** and a salary condition limit that move.

steps.text: Take Mira-approved paid audit course or complete a free course at home
Test AI checks on anonymised old returns each Friday
Apply for higher-paid reviewer vacancies if one appears nearby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is close enough to count on a lease calendar. I would look at my bank balance before I looked at any shiny demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say our clients deserve a named human who can explain a tax decision, even if AGI does the calculations. I would not tell the team robots in 2031 save an accounting job that is already on a screen in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the firm could cut most of our preparation and review fees in 2028, including my role. My daily AI habit helps me notice the change early, but it does not give me two years of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, in 2026, I would stop paying for the extra flat space I barely use and put that money into a cash buffer. I would ask Mira for paid time to learn client representation and complex disputes; in the first year after 2028 I would take any retained client-facing work at the firm while applying for a better-paid vacancy outside routine tax preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am frightened by the speed because the lease is twelve months and the warning is only two years. I can make a plan, but I cannot make two years into five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my flatmate Lea before renewal that I need the smaller room next year. Cutting that bill is more certain than guessing what salary a new field might pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Mira cannot fund that training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the professional body's low-cost short course and keep searching for client representation posts with a stated wage above mine. I would not quit first; that would burn the only pay cheque I have.

say: I would insist clients still need a **named accountant** to explain tax decisions.
I would say **2028** threatens our screen work before capable robots arrive around 2031.
think: I expect much of our **fee work** to disappear, including my preparation and review role.
My daily AI use gives warning, but **thin savings** cannot buy much time.
do: Switch to the **smaller room** before my lease renews.
Seek **paid training** in client representation and disputes, using a low-cost course if refused.
Keep retained client work while applying only for **higher-paid** nonroutine vacancies after 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the likely pay loss and short lease horizon.
S2.quote: I cannot make two years into five.
fieldNote: He distinguishes the **2028 desk shock** from robots expected around 2031; the latter do not shelter accounting work.
His first move is a **certain rent cut**, while retraining depends on paid time or a cheap professional course.

steps.text: Take the smaller room when the lease renews
Request paid client representation training or take low-cost course
Apply for higher-paid nonroutine vacancies after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give me several tax seasons to change my work. I would still want proof that a new role pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues five years is enough to build a proper transition, if the firm shares the gains instead of letting everyone guess. Tax preparation is still screen work, so robots arriving in 2034 are beside the point for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job could still vanish in 2031, but five years lets me change what clients know me for. I would rather be the accountant who handles difficult conversations than the person fastest at drafting a return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I would put one evening a week into dispute and client meeting skills, using the professional body’s low-cost modules. I would ask for and take a paid transfer into advisory work if offered after the next busy season; if AGI arrives in 2031, I would try to keep clients through that first year while the firm decides whether it still needs my post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though less trapped than in the 2028 picture. Five years could let my savings reach several months if rent stays manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a full new degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, another degree would empty the buffer before it exists. I would use short modules, client meetings, and work that the firm pays me to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if advisory work also shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would apply for a compliance role with a published salary before leaving the firm. I cannot treat any job title as a shelter without seeing a real opening.

say: I would tell colleagues **five years** allows a planned transition if training is funded.
I would say robots around **2034** do little for accountants whose work is on screens.
think: My preparation role may still **disappear** in 2031.
I could become known for **client disputes** while building several months of savings.
do: Take **low-cost modules** and one evening of dispute practice weekly.
Take a **paid advisory transfer** if offered; keep serving clients during the first year after 2031.
Apply for a **published-salary compliance opening** if advisory work shrinks, before leaving the firm.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough time to shape a credible plan.
S3.quote: I would use short modules, client meetings, and work that the firm pays me to learn.
fieldNote: He rejects a costly second degree because **cash reserves** are still nearly absent.
He treats advisory as an experiment, with a **published-salary** compliance opening as a conditional fallback.

steps.text: Complete low-cost dispute modules one evening each week
Take paid advisory transfer after busy season if offered
Keep serving clients through first year after 2031 while firm decides staffing
Apply for published-salary compliance vacancy if advisory work shrinks, before leaving firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels like a span I can actually use. I would have to keep my saving habit for it to mean anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell friends a decade is long enough to change a career without pretending the accounting desk stays as it is. Our accounts and returns face AGI in 2036; hands-on robots around 2039 are a different clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I would still expect the core fee work to contract, but I would be 37 by then, not 27. A real cash reserve and several years of client experience would let me choose instead of chasing the first opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Mira this year for supervised client meetings on paid time and join them if she approves, while adding to the rent buffer. By the first year after 2036 I would seek a paid client liaison role if one exists; if not, I would apply to a posted role with a salary above my current pay before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious but steadier because ten years could make the finances real. I would not borrow against an imagined future job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cash goal be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would aim for six months of expenses before taking any voluntary move. The firm pays below the going rate now, so I would review that target every year rather than promise a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays important in the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a small business owner asks why a bill changed, I want to be the one who can explain the numbers plainly. That is a skill worth building even if the final job name changes.

say: I would tell friends a **decade** permits career changes before 2036.
I would separate AGI hitting **accounting desks** in 2036 from robots arriving near 2039.
think: Core accounting **fees** may shrink even with ten years to plan.
A six-month **cash reserve** and client experience could give me choices.
do: Join **supervised client meetings** on paid time if Mira approves.
Build a **six-month reserve** before any voluntary move.
Seek a **paid liaison role** after 2036, applying to higher-paid posted vacancies if needed.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but able to prepare without gambling the rent.
S4.quote: I would not borrow against an imagined future job.
fieldNote: His ten-year plan depends on **earned savings**, not a forecast that client-facing roles are safe.
He wants to keep explaining numbers to clients, while insisting on a **posted salary** before changing employers.

steps.text: Join supervised client meetings on paid time if Mira approves
Build six months of expenses before a voluntary move
Seek paid liaison role after 2036; otherwise apply only above current salary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the whole accounts desk could change before I build a cushion. Paid time to learn client disputes, a clear decision about which jobs the firm will retain, and a temporary income bridge if posts vanish would help. I would still need to see actual vacancies and salaries before moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets the software savings. If the firm cuts the trainee place and pays me the same to cover more clients, the cheerful talk about efficiency will ring hollow. I want Mira to show the team the numbers.

headlineQuote: If the firm cuts the trainee place and pays me the same to cover more clients, the cheerful talk about efficiency will ring hollow.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** accountant who leads three people after earning a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
He uses **AI daily** for checks, yet reviews returns himself and enjoys explaining numbers to clients.
His below-standard **pay**, under-one-month savings, and few nearby firms make even mild change threatening.
A fast **2028** shock sends him toward cheaper rent and funded training; longer warnings give him time to build a reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his desk work before he can save enough to absorb a pay gap.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid dispute training**, clear retained-job decisions, and a temporary income bridge if posts disappear.
